metadata.title: Claude, Client Intake.
metadata.purpose: Answer what a legal client-intake process has to get right first: not writing down the story, but catching a conflict of interest before hearing too much of it. Lands the carry-out that the conflict check comes before the details, not after.

beats.narration_text: A newcomer to a legal practice sees client intake as paperwork — write down what the prospective client says, keep it neat, file it. That misreads the machinery entirely. The actual job is a gate: catch a conflict of interest before hearing anything you can't unhear. Liam, in for Bear — let's take it apart.

beats.narration_text: Here's the natural first read of the mechanism: intake means getting the story down carefully — what happened, in the client's own words. Now watch it break. The firm already represents the other side in this exact dispute. That flawless summary is now worthless — the notes get sealed, and the meeting should never have gone that far. They optimized around the wrong first question. What intake actually has to nail before anything else is one thing: who is on the other side.

shot.new_visual_element: A 'notes' card filling with careful handwriting; the whole card sealed shut the moment a matching name appears beneath it

production_viz.label: A flawless summary, sealed
production_viz.mechanic: A card labelled 'INTAKE NOTES' fills line by line with careful handwritten-style text. Beneath it, a small name field appears and lights up as a MATCH. The whole notes card immediately gets a heavy 'SEALED' stamp across it -- all that careful writing now unusable. A caption fades in: 'the meeting should never have gone that far.'

beats.narration_text: Here's how the actual mechanism runs: fixed order, conflict check first — before the facts, before any advice. Watch the anchor. A prospective client calls about a dispute with their landlord and launches straight into the story. The lawyer's next question, cutting across the momentum, isn't 'tell me more.' It's the landlord's name. That name gets checked against the firm's current clients before another word of the case is spoken. They chose the interruption over the flow — because letting the story roll is the failure mode.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- an intake order card (conflict check first, story second); a caller mid-story, paused on one blank field: landlord's name

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one question, asked first
production_viz.mechanic: A vertical order card: step 1 'CONFLICT CHECK' lit and large, step 2 'THE STORY' dim beneath it. THE ANCHOR. A speech-bubble trail representing the caller's story scrolls in from the left, mid-sentence, then freezes. A single blank field appears, labelled 'landlord's name', outlined only, waiting. THIS BLANK FIELD RETURNS, FILLED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: The name comes back a match — the firm already represents that landlord in an unrelated matter. Conflict flagged, mechanism working exactly as designed: no privileged detail was on record when the flag went up. Now the design is honest about its own limits. A name that doesn't match anyone yet isn't a clean bill — the other side might be a subsidiary of an existing client under a different name, so the check reruns whenever a new name surfaces. And 'no conflict' isn't 'take the case' — capacity, expertise, and fee still get their own separate call. The gate stops the wrong cases; it doesn't decide the right ones.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the blank field lights up 'MATCH FOUND'; then split into a 'no match yet is not clear' card and a 'clear is not take the case' card

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- match found, and its limits
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 BLANK FIELD RETURNS, identical placement, and fills in with 'landlord's name' then flashes 'MATCH FOUND' in the accent colour, before the story trail resumes. It splits into two cards: left reads 'no match yet' with 'CLEAR' dimmed beneath it, labelled 'not proof there's no conflict'; right reads 'conflict clear' with 'TAKE THE CASE?' dimmed beneath it, labelled 'still needs capacity, expertise, fee'.

beats.narration_text: Client intake isn't writing down the story — it's catching the conflict before you've heard too much of it. A gatekeeping question asked after the details always arrives too late.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt — paste it into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I run a small legal practice. Before my next intake call with a new prospective client, act as my first-pass screen, not my counsel: draft the exact opening script that gets the other side's name and any known aliases out of the caller before they launch into the story; give me the checklist that name gets run against — current clients, adverse parties on active matters, known subsidiaries — before another word about the case; and name the exact moment I should stop the call cold and refer the prospective client out. Go deeper: in your own work, what's the equivalent gatekeeping question — the thing that has to be checked before any information flows — and are you actually asking it first, or letting the story roll? Liam, in for Bear.
